units.title: Convexity, optimality conditions and conditioning
outcomes: Prove the first- and second-order characterizations of a differentiable convex function on an open convex domain.
Distinguish stationary points, local minima and global minima, including degenerate Hessians.
Read smoothness, strong convexity and conditioning from a quadratic's eigenvalues.
units.why: An optimizer's behavior starts with the objective's geometry. These conditions tell you which local evidence certifies a global solution and which does not.

next.note: Apply curvature and conditioning to ridge regression.

study.title: EE364a: convex sets and convex functions
study.locator: Lecture 2 notes: Convex set (slide 2-3), Convex combination and convex hull (2-4), Hyperplanes and halfspaces (2-6), and Intersection (2-12)
study.depth: Read these headings only. Use the book below for the proofs; leave separation and generalized inequalities aside.

study.title: EE364a: derivative tests for convexity
study.locator: Lectures 3 and 4 notes: First-order condition (slide 3-7), Second-order conditions (3-8), and Examples (3-9): quadratic and least-squares functions

study.title: Convexity proofs and curvature bounds
study.locator: Sections 2.1.4 (pp. 23 to 25), 3.1.1 to 3.1.4 (pp. 67 to 71), 4.2.3 through Unconstrained problems (pp. 139 to 141), and 9.1.2 (pp. 459 to 463)
study.depth: Prove the derivative tests using restrictions to lines. In 9.1.2 focus on the lower and upper quadratic models and the ratio \(M/m\), not the width calculation.

focus: A convex set contains every segment between its points. A convex function has a convex domain and lies below each chord; its tangent planes lie below its graph.

For \(C^2\) functions on an open convex domain, a PSD Hessian everywhere characterizes convexity. At one stationary point, a PSD Hessian is only a necessary local-minimum condition; a PD Hessian is sufficient.

For \(f(x)=x^\top Qx/2\) with symmetric positive definite \(Q\), \(\mu=\lambda_{\min}(Q)\), \(L=\lambda_{\max}(Q)\), and \(\kappa=L/\mu\). The gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz and the lower quadratic model uses \(\mu/2\).
units.reproduce: Closed-book, prove the first-order inequality in both directions, then prove the Hessian test by restricting to a segment. By hand use \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(1,9)\): find \(\operatorname{grad} f\), \(\mu=1\), \(L=9\), \(\kappa=9\) and \(f(1,1)=5\). Check with NumPy float64 arrays, np.linalg.eigvalsh(Q) and np.linalg.cond(Q); scalar absolute differences from [1,9], 9 and 5 must be below 1e-12. No random draws are needed.
traps: Dropping the convex-domain assumption: \(1/x^2\) has positive second derivative on its disconnected domain, but that domain is not convex.
Calling every stationary point a minimum: \(x^2-y^2\) has a saddle at the origin.
Equating strict and strong convexity: \(x^4\) is strictly convex on \(\mathbb{R}\) but has no positive global lower curvature bound.

selfTest.q: Where are the assumptions used in the first-order proof?
selfTest.a: Convexity of the domain keeps \(x+t(y-x)\) inside it. Convexity of \(f\) supplies the chord inequality; divide by positive \(t\) and use differentiability as \(t\) tends to zero. Conversely, apply the tangent inequality at \(z=\theta x+(1-\theta)y\) to \(x\) and \(y\). Nonnegative weights preserve inequalities and cancel the derivative terms; domain convexity ensures \(z\) exists. At \(\theta=0\) or \(1\) the chord statement is equality.

selfTest.q: Why does a zero gradient certify a global minimum only in the convex case?
selfTest.a: The convex tangent lower bound becomes \(f(y)\ge f(x)\) for every feasible \(y\). Without convexity that lower bound need not hold; \(-x^2\) has zero derivative at its maximum.

selfTest.q: Does a zero Hessian at a stationary point settle local optimality?
selfTest.a: No. At zero, \(x^4\) has a minimum and \(-x^4\) has a maximum; both have zero derivative and zero second derivative.

selfTest.q: Why is \(\mu>0\) needed for uniqueness?
selfTest.a: The strong-convexity midpoint inequality subtracts \(\mu\|x-y\|_2^2/8\). Two distinct minimizers would therefore give a midpoint below the optimal value. Convexity keeps the midpoint feasible; \(\mu>0\) makes the subtraction strictly positive.

practice.name: Convex Optimization: Exercise 3.8, Second-order condition for convexity
practice.note: Attempt both directions before looking back at the first-order proof on p. 70. Give the disconnected-domain counterexample as well.

units.stopWhen: You can prove both derivative tests with their domain assumptions, classify the three stationary-point counterexamples, and recover the quadratic's curvature bounds without notes.

fit.note: Kept: EE364a and the book supply definitions, checkable proofs, quadratic geometry and a named proof exercise within five hours.

study.title: Heavy-ball dynamics on quadratics
study.locator: Sections 12.6.1.2 to 12.6.1.4 and 12.6.3.1 to 12.6.3.2; PyTorch momentum_2d cell

focus: In the eigenbasis, GD errors obey \(e_{k+1,i}=(1-\eta\lambda_i)e_{k,i}\). Uniform convergence for all starts requires \(0<\eta<2/L\); \(\eta=2/(L+\mu)\) minimizes the worst factor to \((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)\).

Heavy-ball uses \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta\operatorname{grad} f(x_k)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\). Each eigenmode has characteristic polynomial \(r^2-(1+\beta-\eta\lambda)r+\beta\); repeated roots can produce a transient \(kr^k\) factor.

For \(f=(1/n)\sum f_i\) and independent uniform indices, the minibatch average gradient is unbiased and has covariance \(\Sigma/B\). Sampling without replacement has a finite-population correction; reshuffling is not independent sampling.
On a general \(L\)-smooth lower-bounded objective, the descent lemma controls objective decrease, not global optimality. Report full-objective residuals separately from noisy minibatch gradients.
units.reproduce: By hand derive the GD eigenmode recurrence and heavy-ball polynomial. In NumPy float64 use \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(1,9)\), \(x_0=(1,1)\), \(x_{-1}=x_0\). After ten updates, GD with \(\eta=0.2\) has \(\|x_{10}\|_2=0.151850025\) and \(\|x_{10}\|_2/\|x_0\|_2=0.1073741824=0.8^{10}\) in exact arithmetic (measured absolute discrepancy 1.4e-17, allow 1e-12). Heavy-ball with \(\eta=0.25\) and \(\beta=0.25\) has \(\|x_{10}\|_2=0.0166875073\). At \(\eta=2/9\) GD's second coordinate alternates without shrinking; at \(\eta=0.23\) its magnitude after ten steps is 1.96715136. Then create rng=np.random.default_rng(5); make its only draw noise=rng.standard_normal((10000,4),dtype=np.float64), in array row order. np.var(noise[:,0],ddof=1) is 0.984311 and np.var(noise.mean(axis=1),ddof=1) is 0.251557. Derive the theoretical variances 1 and 1/4; these measured values are not exact theoretical equalities. Allow absolute 1e-6 for the displayed simulation values.
traps: Including \(2/L\) in the convergent interval. The largest-curvature mode has multiplier -1 there.
Claiming momentum contracts by its asymptotic spectral radius at every step. Repeated roots and initial state affect transients.
Calling the squared-gradient moment a noise variance, or assuming four correlated gradients reduce variance by four. Independence matters.

selfTest.q: Why is the quadratic rate a Euclidean error rate, not the same objective-gap rate?
selfTest.a: Symmetry gives an orthonormal eigenbasis; positivity gives eigenvalues in \([\mu,L]\). Every error multiplier has magnitude at most \(\rho\), hence \(\|e_k\|_2\le\rho^k\|e_0\|_2\), including the base case \(k=0\). The quadratic gap weights squared errors, so it contracts by at most \(\rho^{2k}\).

selfTest.q: What happens at \(\eta=2/L\) if the initial error has no largest-eigenvalue component?
selfTest.a: It may still converge in the remaining modes. The strict bound guarantees convergence for every initial error, rather than claiming every start fails at the boundary.

selfTest.q: Why does minibatch covariance divide by B?
selfTest.a: Center each gradient and expand the covariance of their average. Independence makes cross-covariances zero; identical sampling gives \(B\) diagonal terms \(\Sigma\), divided by \(B^2\). Unbiasedness follows from uniform sampling of the average objective.

selfTest.q: Does constant-step SGD converge exactly when additive gradient noise persists?
selfTest.a: Generally no. For scalar curvature \(\lambda\), independent zero-mean noise variance \(\sigma^2\) and \(|1-\eta\lambda|<1\) give limiting error variance \(\eta\sigma^2/(\lambda(2-\eta\lambda))\). The variance recurrence adds \(\eta^2\sigma^2\) at every step.

practice.name: D2L: momentum on multiple eigenvalues

study.title: Gradient-norm clipping contract
study.locator: clip_grad_norm_: concatenated-gradient norm, in-place modification, max_norm, norm_type and error_if_nonfinite

focus: With \(m_0=0\), \(m_t=(1-\beta_1)\sum_{i=1}^t\beta_1^{t-i}g_i\). Constant \(\mathbb{E}[g_i]=\bar{g}\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[m_t]=(1-\beta_1^t)\bar{g}\); constant \(\mathbb{E}[g_i^2]\) gives the analogous second-moment correction. Independence is not needed for these expectations.
Correction normalizes the finite weights. It does not make \(\hat{m}/\sqrt{\hat{v}}\) an unbiased gradient estimate when gradients change or the denominator is random.

Clipping projects \(g\) onto a Euclidean ball: \(g\min(1,c/\|g\|_2)\), with zero mapped to zero. Clip before updating moments. AdamW shrinks parameters separately; adding \(\lambda\theta\) to \(g\) changes both moments instead.

A schedule needs a clock and restart state. A small step caused by a tiny learning rate is not evidence of stationarity; check the un-clipped full-objective gradient and use the residual unit's stopping contract.
units.reproduce: Derive the finite-sum correction by induction, checking \(t=1\). For constant \(g=(2,-1)\), \(\beta_1=0.9\) and \(\beta_2=0.999\), hand-compute \(m_3=(0.542,-0.271)\) and \(v_3=(0.011988004,0.002997001)\); corrected moments are (2,-1) and (4,1) in exact arithmetic. Check in NumPy float64 with infinity-norm tolerance 1e-12. Then run ten float64 updates on \(f(\theta)=(\theta_1^2+9\theta_2^2)/2\) from (1,-2), \(m_0=v_0=0\), \(\epsilon=10^{-6}\), decay=0.1, \(\mathit{lr}_t=0.01/(1+0.1(t-1))\), \(t=1,\ldots,10\). Clip \(g\) to Euclidean norm 1 using the exact formula above; update moments, then \(\theta=(1-\mathit{lr}_t\cdot 0.1)\theta-\mathit{lr}_t\hat{m}/(\sqrt{\hat{v}}+\epsilon)\). Result: (0.92127176,-1.91402438), allowing 1e-8 in infinity norm for the displayed rounding. Compare torch.optim.AdamW on CPU with float64, the same clipped gradients, betas=(0.9,0.999), eps=1e-6, weight_decay=0.1, foreach=False and the same per-update lr. On PyTorch 2.14.1 the measured infinity-norm difference is 2.22e-16; allow 1e-12. Do not substitute clip_grad_norm_ in this oracle comparison, because its stabilizing denominator changes the mathematical projection slightly. Save \(\theta\),\(m\),\(v\),\(t\) and the schedule clock after step five and check resumed versus uninterrupted final states within 1e-12. No random draws are needed.
traps: Starting the bias-correction clock at zero, or incrementing it once per coordinate instead of once per update.
Putting \(\epsilon\) inside the square root while claiming the Adam formula with \(\epsilon\) outside it.
Restoring parameters but not moments and the schedule clock. The next update is then a different algorithmic state.

selfTest.q: What assumptions does the bias-correction derivation actually use?
selfTest.a: Zero initial moments remove a \(\beta^tm_0\) term. Constant \(\beta\) in \([0,1)\) supplies the finite geometric sum and a nonzero denominator for \(t\ge 1\). Equal first or second moments of the gradient sequence let expectation factor out of the weighted sum. Independence is not required.

selfTest.q: Why is Adam's vhat not the gradient variance?
selfTest.a: It estimates an uncentered second moment. Variance subtracts the square of the mean; vhat does not.

selfTest.q: When does coupled \(L_2\) match decoupled decay?
selfTest.a: For plain SGD with no momentum or preconditioner, \(\theta-\eta(g+\lambda\theta)\) equals \((1-\eta\lambda)\theta-\eta g\) in exact arithmetic. Adaptive scaling or momentum generally destroys this equivalence.

selfTest.q: What is the norm-clipping solution for \(g=(3,4)\) and \(c=2\)?
selfTest.a: Its norm is 5, so the projection is (1.2,1.6). Clamping each coordinate to [-2,2] gives (2,2), which is a different projection and exceeds norm 2.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: implement adaptive updates, clipping and update-indexed schedules; test finite-sum moments, checkpoint/resume and an un-clipped stationarity residual on the same deterministic quadratic.
units.stopWhen: You can derive the correction with its assumptions and pass moment, decay-placement and restart tests, including the 1e-12 infinity-norm oracle comparison.

study.title: Proximal maps, soft thresholding and lasso
study.locator: Sections 1.1 (p. 124), 4.2 (pp. 148 to 151), 6.5.2 (p. 188, equation 6.9), and 7.1's lasso formulation (p. 196)
study.depth: In 4.2 read the basic update and quadratic upper-model interpretation. Skip accelerated methods and ADMM. In 6.5.2 stop before projection onto the \(\ell_1\) ball. Skip 7.1.1 on p. 197: it prints \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}=S_\gamma\) although \(g=\gamma\|x\|_1\); the correct general scaling is \(\operatorname{prox}_{\eta g}=S_{\eta\gamma}\). Its Gram rewrite with \(\tilde{b}=A^\top b\) also fails to preserve the linear term, already for \(A=[2]\), \(b=[1]\). Derive lasso's update from 4.2 and 6.5.2 instead.

focus: Write inequalities as \(f_i(x)\le 0\) and attach nonnegative multipliers. The dual function minimizes the Lagrangian over \(x\) without imposing the original constraints; weak duality gives a lower bound.

KKT comprises primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity and complementary slackness. For a differentiable convex problem with affine equalities, KKT is sufficient; Slater's condition supplies necessity and dual attainment when a primal optimum exists.

For \(0.5\|Aw-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|w\|_1\), proximal gradient takes \(u=w-\eta A^\top(Aw-b)\), then \(w+=\operatorname{sign}(u)\max(|u|-\eta\lambda,0)\). The threshold scales with \(\eta\), not just \(\lambda\).

At zero, the \(\ell_1\) subgradient is the interval \([-1,1]\). Derive the three scalar cases instead of pretending \(\operatorname{abs}\) has a unique derivative there. For the smooth part, \(\eta\le 1/\|A\|_2^2\) gives the quadratic upper-model descent argument.

In CVXPY 1.9.3 use float64 a, z=cp.Variable(2), constraints=[z>=0,cp.sum(z)==1], objective=cp.Minimize(0.5*cp.sum_squares(z-a)); form prob=cp.Problem(objective,constraints) and call prob.solve(solver='CLARABEL',tol_gap_abs=1e-10,tol_gap_rel=1e-10,tol_feas=1e-10,max_iter=100). traps: Giving \(x\ge 0\) the wrong multiplier sign. Its standard-form constraint is \(-x\le 0\), so stationarity contains \(-\lambda\).
Inferring a positive multiplier from an active constraint. Complementary slackness only says a positive multiplier implies activity, not the converse.
Using ridge's shrinkage as lasso's proximal operator. Ridge scales coordinates continuously; lasso thresholds a whole interval to zero.

selfTest.q: Where does each assumption enter the KKT sufficiency proof?
selfTest.a: Convex objective and inequality functions, affine equalities, and nonnegative multipliers make \(L\) convex in \(x\). Differentiability and stationarity therefore minimize \(L\) globally. Feasibility and complementary slackness make \(L(x^*)=f(x^*)\). The dual infimum is then \(f(x^*)\), so weak duality certifies optimality. Slater is not needed for sufficiency.

selfTest.q: Does this QP satisfy Slater's condition?
selfTest.a: Yes. \(x=(0.5,0.5)\) strictly satisfies \(-x<0\) and satisfies the affine equality. This supplies the constraint qualification; the strictly convex objective also makes the primal optimizer unique.

selfTest.q: Why is the proximal minimizer zero when \(|u|\le\eta\lambda\)?
selfTest.a: At \(w=0\) the stationarity inclusion is \(0\in -u+\eta\lambda[-1,1]\), exactly that inequality. The quadratic term is strictly convex, so this condition identifies the unique minimizer, including both threshold endpoints.

selfTest.q: How can you check a lasso answer without knowing w*?
selfTest.a: Let \(h=A^\top(Aw-b)\). Nonzero coordinates need \(h_i+\lambda\operatorname{sign}(w_i)=0\); zero coordinates need \(|h_i|\le\lambda\). Check these residuals with a stated numerical zero threshold, or use \(\|w-S_{\eta\lambda}(w-\eta h)\|/\eta\) as a proximal-gradient residual.

study.title: A quasi-Newton comparison with an analytic gradient
study.locator: BFGS method; options gtol, maxiter, c1, c2 and hess_inv0; Notes on precision loss
study.depth: Use the default line-search parameters and initial inverse-Hessian approximation. Do not study or implement a full BFGS convergence proof here.

focus: Minimizing the local quadratic model gives \(Hp=-g\). Solve this system instead of forming \(H^{-1}\). Positive definite \(H\) makes \(g^\top p<0\) for nonzero \(g\); an indefinite Hessian does not.

A Lipschitz Hessian and a uniformly bounded inverse Hessian near a nondegenerate minimizer give a quadratic error bound for full Newton steps, once the starting point is close enough. Backtracking handles the approach to that neighborhood.

Quasi-Newton methods replace freshly evaluated curvature with an approximation informed by gradient changes. Their iteration count alone hides line-search evaluations; BFGS is an oracle here, not a second implementation assignment.
units.reproduce: By hand minimize \(\phi(x)=x^4/4+x^2/2-2x\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Its gradient is \(x^3+x-2\), Hessian \(3x^2+1\), and unique minimizer \(x^*=1\). Derive Newton's update and the exact recurrence \(e_{\text{next}}=e^2(2x+1)/(3x^2+1)\), where \(e=x-1\). Starting at \(x_0=1.5\), use NumPy float64 for four updates: absolute errors after each are 0.1290322581, 0.01124439868, 9.394478985e-5 and 6.618699366e-9. Compare each displayed error with absolute tolerance 1e-10. The first four ratios \(|e_{\text{next}}|/e^2\) are 0.516129, 0.675367, 0.743020 and 0.749941, approaching 3/4; stop the rate measurement before rounding dominates. With SciPy 1.18.1, call minimize on the same scalar objective with x0=np.array([1.5],dtype=np.float64), jac returning np.array([x[0]**3+x[0]-2],dtype=np.float64), method='BFGS', options={'gtol':1e-10,'maxiter':100}. It reports success, eight iterations, nine function and nine gradient evaluations, and gradient infinity norm 1.32e-13. Require \(|x-1|\le 10^{-9}\) and \(\|\operatorname{grad}\|_\infty \le 10^{-10}\); compare work at that residual, counting Newton's derivative and Hessian calls too. Do not infer a timing advantage. No random draws are needed.
traps: Applying the rootfinding Newton formula to \(\phi\) rather than \(\phi'\). That finds a zero of the loss, not its stationary point.
Claiming quadratic convergence at a multiple root, or from every starting point. A vanishing derivative breaks the local denominator bound.
Counting BFGS iterations while ignoring its line-search calls, or interpreting solver success without checking the returned gradient.

selfTest.q: Why does this example converge to 1 from 1.5?
selfTest.a: For \(x>1\), the recurrence gives \(e_{\text{next}}>0\). Also \(e_{\text{next}}/e=(x-1)(2x+1)/(3x^2+1)<1\) because the denominator minus the numerator is \(x^2+x+2>0\). The iterates decrease and stay above 1; their limit must solve \(x^3+x-2=0\). Positive Hessian makes that root unique. Dividing the recurrence by \(e^2\) gives the limit 3/4.

selfTest.q: Where are the local Newton proof assumptions used?
selfTest.a: A Lipschitz Hessian bounds the Taylor remainder by a constant times \(\|e\|_2^2\). Nonsingularity and local inverse bounds keep solving with \(H\) from amplifying it without limit. A sufficiently close start keeps the iterates in that neighborhood; full steps give the Newton error cancellation.

selfTest.q: What happens to Newton rootfinding for \(F(x)=(x-r)^2\)?
selfTest.a: For \(x\ne r\) the update is \(x_{\text{next}}=x-(x-r)/2\), so \(e_{\text{next}}=e/2\): linear, not quadratic. The simple-root assumption fails because \(F'(r)=0\).

selfTest.q: Must a Newton direction descend at a stationary saddle?
selfTest.a: No. At a stationary point \(g=0\), the Newton step is zero when the Hessian is invertible, even if the point is a saddle. Away from it, an indefinite Hessian can also give a non-descent direction.

units.title: Floating point, rounding, overflow and cancellation
outcomes: Derive spacing and unit roundoff from a binary significand and distinguish precision from exponent range.
Compare float64, float32, float16 and bfloat16, including normal and subnormal values.
Construct overflow, underflow and cancellation failures and check an algebraically stable alternative.
units.why: Mathematical real arithmetic is not a machine's arithmetic. A dtype's range and spacing predict different failures, and rewriting a formula can matter more than increasing precision.

next.note: Use constructed failure mechanisms to interpret non-finite diagnostics.
Apply range-versus-precision reasoning when selecting dtypes.

study.title: Binary representation and rounding
study.locator: Section 1.1: Definitions 1.1.1 to 1.1.2, equations 1.1.1 to 1.1.6, and Sections 1.1.2 to 1.1.3
study.depth: Use the Python examples. The main-text minimum-range discussion concerns normal values; read footnote 2 and the dtype reference below before treating \(\mathit{tiny}\) as the smallest positive representable value. Skip the Julia-specific Exercise 1.1.5.

study.title: Conditioning and unstable cancellation
study.locator: Sections 1.2.1 to 1.2.2, condition numbers and error estimates, on the preceding Problems and conditioning page; Section 1.4.1 and Examples 1.4.1 to 1.4.2 on Stability
study.depth: Focus on subtractive cancellation and the stable quadratic-root rewrite; skip the later polynomial-root perturbation demo.

study.title: Inspect low-precision formats
study.locator: torch.finfo: bits, eps, max, tiny, smallest_normal and the note about subnormal numbers

focus: With \(p\) total significand bits including the hidden leading one, spacing in \([2^e,2^{e+1})\) is \(2^{e-(p-1)}\). \(\mathit{eps}\) is the gap above 1; unit roundoff for round-to-nearest is \(\mathit{eps}/2\). The relative bound needs normal-range results and no overflow.
float64, float32, float16 and bfloat16 have \(p=53,24,11,8\) and exponent fields of 11,8,5,8 bits respectively. bfloat16 has wide range but coarser spacing than float16.

Overflow produces infinities; gradual underflow first reaches subnormals with reduced relative precision. \(\mathit{tiny}\) is the smallest positive normal, not the smallest positive representable value.

Subtracting nearby rounded operands can destroy relative accuracy even when the subtraction itself is exact. Separate conditioning of the requested difference from avoidable instability in how its operands were formed.
units.reproduce: By hand enumerate the \(d=4\) fractional-bit system in FNC Exercise 1.1.1 and derive its spacing. Then use np.finfo for np.float64, np.float32 and np.float16, and torch.finfo(torch.bfloat16) on CPU for bfloat16. Print eps, tiny and max to three significant digits: float64 (2.22e-16,2.23e-308,1.80e308), float32 (1.19e-7,1.18e-38,3.40e38), float16 (9.77e-4,6.10e-5,6.55e4), bfloat16 (7.81e-3,1.18e-38,3.39e38). Derive \(\mathit{eps}=2^{-(p-1)}\) and check each \(\mathit{eps}\) within relative scalar tolerance 1e-6. Inspect np.nextafter(dtype(0),dtype(1)), and torch.nextafter on CPU bfloat16 scalars, to see values below \(\mathit{tiny}\). In NumPy float64 set x=np.float64(1e8): \(\sqrt{x^2+1}-x\) returns 0, while \(1/(\sqrt{x^2+1}+x)\) returns about 5.00e-9. Rationalize the expression by hand and bound the exact result's difference from \(1/(2x)\) by \(1/(8x^3)\); allow absolute 1e-20 for the stable scalar. Finally evaluate np.exp(np.float64(1000)) and np.exp(np.float64(-1000)) inside np.errstate(over='ignore',under='ignore'): outputs are inf and 0. These are range failures, not exact evaluations of \(\exp\). No random draws are needed.
traps: Calling \(\mathit{eps}\) the smallest representable number, or calling finfo.tiny the smallest subnormal.
Assuming bfloat16 is more precise because its exponent range is larger.
Applying a relative error tolerance at a true zero, or claiming that a stable rewrite recovers information already rounded out of its inputs.

selfTest.q: Why is round-to-nearest error bounded by eps/2 in the normal range?
selfTest.a: In each binade the absolute error is at most half its spacing. Dividing by \(|x|\ge 2^e\) bounds relative error by \(2^{-(p-1)}/2\). The lower bound on \(|x|\) uses normal binade representation; subnormals instead have fixed absolute spacing. Overflow is excluded.

selfTest.q: What is lost in \(\sqrt{x^2+1}-x\) at \(x=10^8\)?
selfTest.a: \(x^2\) is about \(10^{16}\), where float64 spacing is 2, so adding 1 rounds away under ties-to-even. The square root returns \(x\) and subtraction gives zero. Rationalization avoids subtracting nearly equal operands; it does not make \(x^2+1\) exact.

selfTest.q: Is the computed zero an underflow of the true answer?
selfTest.a: No. The true answer is about 5e-9, well within the normal float64 range. It is cancellation after an earlier rounding loss.

selfTest.q: Can \((1+\mathit{eps}/2)-1\) and \(1+(\mathit{eps}/2-1)\) differ in float64?
selfTest.a: Yes. Under round-to-nearest ties-to-even, the first evaluates to zero and the second to about 1.11e-16. The real-arithmetic associative law does not transfer to rounded operations.

units.title: Stable log-sum-exp, online reductions and mixed precision
outcomes: Derive log-sum-exp's shift identity, max bounds and convexity without relying on a loss implementation.
Implement naive, balanced pairwise and Kahan reductions and distinguish an error bound from a measured error.
Prove online mean and centered-sum invariants and test low-precision storage with higher-precision accumulation.

Apply the distinction between storage precision and accumulation precision.
Use stable log probabilities and controlled reductions when aggregating likelihoods.

study.title: Log-sum-exp as a smooth convex maximum
study.locator: Section 3.1.5: Log-sum-exp bounds on p. 72 and the Hessian/Cauchy-Schwarz proof on p. 74

study.title: Summation trees and compensation
study.locator: Section 2 (pp. 784 to 786), especially equations 2.1 to 2.6; Section 3's general error expression and pairwise summation (pp. 787 to 788) and Kahan's compensated summation (pp. 790 to 791, equation 3.10 on p. 791)

study.title: Online mean and centered second moment
study.locator: Opening cancellation example and recurrence formulas for \(M_k\), \(S_k\) and sample variance \(S_k/(k-1)\)
study.depth: Stop before the C++ RunningStat class. Prove the invariant in exact arithmetic before translating it to NumPy. A variance can be zero, and overflow can still occur.

study.title: Precision budget for inputs and accumulators
study.locator: torch.finfo: eps, max and smallest_normal for float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64

focus: For finite nonempty \(x\), \(\operatorname{LSE}(x)=m+\log(\sum\exp(x_i-m))\), \(m=\max x\). Every exponential is \(\le 1\) and at least one is 1, giving \(m\le\operatorname{LSE}\le m+\log(n)\). The Hessian \(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\) is PSD by a weighted-variance argument.

With unit roundoff \(u\), no overflow or underflow and \((n-1)u<1\), recursive summation has absolute error \(\le\gamma_{n-1}\sum|x_i|\), \(\gamma_k=ku/(1-ku)\). A balanced tree shortens rounding paths; it does not remove conditioning from cancellation.

Online mean uses \(\delta=x_n-\mathit{mean}_{\text{old}}\) and \(\mathit{mean}_{\text{new}}=\mathit{mean}_{\text{old}}+\delta/n\). The centered sum updates \(M2_{\text{new}}=M2_{\text{old}}+\delta(x_n-\mathit{mean}_{\text{new}})\). Check \(M2_n=\sum(x_i-\mathit{mean}_n)^2\) with base case \(n=1\), and divide by \(n-1\) only for sample variance with \(n\ge 2\).

Higher-precision accumulation can prevent repeated rounding of the running total. It cannot restore detail lost when input values were quantized; distinguish operand, product and accumulator precision.
units.reproduce: Derive the \(\operatorname{LSE}\) max bounds and Hessian PSD proof, and prove the online centered-sum invariant by induction. Hand-check data [1,2,3]: mean=2, M2=2, sample variance=1. In NumPy float64 use x=[1000,1001,999]; the shifted formula gives 1001.4076059644, allowing 1e-10 absolute error for this displayed rounding. Compare the unrounded result with scipy.special.logsumexp on SciPy 1.18.1: measured absolute difference is 0; require \(\le 10^{-12}\), not exact equality. Implement a left-to-right sum with float64 accumulator zero, a balanced sum splitting each array at len(a)//2 recursively (empty sum zero, singleton returns its value), and Kahan with s=c=0; for each v use y=v-c, t=s+y, c=(t-s)-y, s=t. On np.concatenate((np.array([1e16],dtype=np.float64),np.ones(1024,dtype=np.float64),np.array([-1e16],dtype=np.float64))), the outputs are 0, 1022 and 1024. Against math.fsum's 1024 the measured absolute errors are 1024, 2 and 0; allow 1e-12 for these displayed checks. Run the online recurrence on [1e8+1,1e8+2,1e8+3] in that order in float64: sample variance is 1, while \((\operatorname{sum}(x^2)-3\operatorname{mean}(x)^2)/2\) gives 0. The absolute difference from np.var(x,ddof=1) for the online result is 0, allowed \(\le 10^{-12}\). Finally sum 4096 float16 ones left-to-right, explicitly casting every updated accumulator to np.float16: the total stalls at 2048. np.sum on those same inputs with dtype=np.float32 gives 4096; measured absolute errors against the integer count are 2048 and 0. No random draws are needed. These examples do not establish that Kahan or an online variance algorithm wins for every input.
traps: Using np.sum as a claimed naive left-to-right baseline. Its reduction strategy depends on axis and layout; implement the order you claim to test.
Rearranging Kahan's compensation into algebraically equivalent operations. Reassociation changes the rounding errors the correction is meant to retain.
Ignoring empty inputs, infinities or the \(n=1\) sample-variance denominator. The finite nonempty \(\operatorname{LSE}\) contract and \(n\ge 2\) variance contract need explicit checks.

selfTest.q: Why is the LSE Hessian positive semidefinite but not positive definite?
selfTest.a: For finite \(x\), \(p_i=\exp(x_i)/\sum\exp(x_j)\) are positive and sum to one. \(v^\top(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top)v=\sum p_i(v_i-\sum p_jv_j)^2\ge 0\). Positivity makes this a weighted variance; constant \(v\) gives zero, so the all-ones direction is a null direction.

selfTest.q: Where does the online centered-sum proof use its assumptions?
selfTest.a: At \(n=1\), \(\mathit{mean}=x_1\) and \(M2=0\). For \(n\ge 2\), the old centered deviations sum to zero, so recentering the first \(n-1\) values adds \((n-1)(\delta/n)^2\) with no cross term. The new deviation is \(\delta(n-1)/n\); adding its square gives \(\delta^2(n-1)/n=\delta(x_n-\mathit{mean}_{\text{new}})\). Division uses \(n>0\); the algebra assumes exact arithmetic, not an exact floating-point invariant.

selfTest.q: Why can a small absolute summation error be a large relative one?
selfTest.a: Cancellation can make \(|\sum x_i|\) tiny while \(\sum|x_i|\) is large. The relative error bound contains their ratio, the summation condition number. At a zero exact sum use an absolute criterion instead.

selfTest.q: Does float32 accumulation make float16 inputs equivalent to original float32 inputs?
selfTest.a: No. It improves the accumulation of already rounded inputs. Any distinction erased by conversion to float16 is still gone, even if every later addition were exact.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: derive and implement a finite-input log-partition primitive, three explicit summation orders and online mean/variance; test cancellation, large offsets, low-precision storage and accumulator choices against independent oracles.
units.stopWhen: Your reduction and online-state tests reproduce the stated absolute errors, and you can prove the \(\operatorname{LSE}\) bounds and centered-sum invariant while explaining which precision losses cannot be repaired.

fit.note: Coverage and depth failed for compensated summation and online centered variance. Higham's analysis and Cook's recurrence fill those gaps; the added dtype contract supports accumulation checks and mini-project practice.

units.title: Residuals, tolerances and iterative-solver error
outcomes: Derive the relationship between a linear-system residual, solution error and conditioning.
Design norm-specific absolute and relative residual tests with meaningful scales.
Distinguish residual convergence, stagnation, non-finite failure and iteration-cap termination.
units.why: A solver stops because of a rule, not because mathematics declares the answer correct. Residual scaling and conditioning tell you what that rule actually certifies.

next.note: Use residual and solution-error checks when comparing linear solvers.
Report convergence and numerical failure as separate statuses.

study.title: Linear residuals and conditioning
study.locator: Section 2.8.1, Theorem 2.8.1; Section 2.8.2, Residual and backward error, Definition 2.8.2 and equation 2.8.11
study.depth: Keep the normwise residual/error relationship. Do not reproduce the later least-squares solver comparison.

study.title: Fixed-point errors versus iteration stopping
study.locator: Sections 4.2.1 to 4.2.3, equations 4.2.2 to 4.2.7, Theorem 4.2.1 and Corollary 4.2.1; then Section 4.3.2's newton stopping implementation
study.depth: Observation 4.2.1 says the iteration diverges for all initial values when \(|g'(p)|>1\); read that as a local statement, since starting at \(p\) stays at \(p\). Theorem 4.2.1 as printed allows any invariant interval, but existence needs completeness: \(x/2\) maps \((0,1)\) into itself with no fixed point there. Read it with \(S\) a closed interval, then finish the existence step yourself in the self-test. Read the scalar stopping loop on the Newton page, not its graphical demos.

study.title: Objective certificates rather than tiny steps
study.locator: Section 5.5.1 (pp. 241 to 242) and Section 9.1.2, equations 9.9 to 9.10 (p. 460) and the strong convexity constants paragraph (p. 463)
study.depth: Read only primal-dual gap stopping and the strong-convexity gradient-to-suboptimality bound, including why an unknown m makes that bound a conceptual rather than practical stopping rule.

focus: For invertible \(A\), \(r=b-A\hat{x}=A(x^*-\hat{x})\). Hence \(\|\hat{x}-x^*\|_2\le\|A^{-1}\|_2\|r\|_2\); when \(b\) and \(x^*\) are nonzero, relative error \(\le\kappa_2(A)\|r\|_2/\|b\|_2\).

A scale-aware residual test is \(\|r\|_2\le\mathit{atol}+\mathit{rtol}\|b\|_2\). State the norm, units, \(\mathit{atol}\) and \(\mathit{rtol}\). The normalized residual \(\|r\|_2/(\|A\|_2\|\hat{x}\|_2+\|b\|_2)\) is a useful normwise backward-error measure, not a forward-error certificate.

For a \(\mu\)-strongly-convex differentiable unconstrained objective, \(\|\operatorname{grad} f(x)\|_2^2/(2\mu)\) bounds the objective gap. Constraints and nonsmooth penalties need KKT or proximal residuals instead; noisy gradients are not exact stationarity residuals.

Check finite values first, then residual convergence, then stagnation and the iteration limit. Small successive steps can reflect poor scaling or rounding. Report the reason for exit rather than labeling every exit converged.
units.reproduce: Derive the residual-to-error bound by hand. In NumPy float64 set A=diag(1,1e-8), xstar=np.ones(2,dtype=np.float64), b=A@xstar and xhat=np.array([1,0],dtype=np.float64). Compute r=b-A@xhat: \(\|r\|_2=10^{-8}\), relative residual=1e-8, relative solution error=0.7071067812, \(\kappa_2(A)=10^8\), and normalized residual=5e-9 using the denominator \(\|A\|_2\|\hat{x}\|_2+\|b\|_2\). Allow relative scalar tolerance 1e-9 for these displayed nonzero quantities. The relative-error bound is 1, so the large observed error does not contradict it. An absolute-only threshold 1e-7 accepts this poor answer. With \(\mathit{atol}=10^{-12}\) and \(\mathit{rtol}=10^{-10}\), the Euclidean residual test rejects it. Multiply both \(A\) and \(b\) by \(10^8\): the residual becomes 1 and the relative residual remains about 1e-8; the same combined test rejects it again. Take one correction xhat+=np.linalg.solve(A,r) using the original A and r. The measured final Euclidean error and residual are both 0; require \(\le 10^{-12}\) rather than exact equality. Finally work the harmonic partial sums \(H_n\) by hand: successive increments tend to zero although \(H_n\) diverges. Use this to justify a stagnation status separate from residual convergence. No random draws are needed.
traps: Treating a tiny residual as a tiny solution error without checking the inverse sensitivity or condition number.
Using a relative-only tolerance when the target scale is zero, or comparing residuals in different units without rescaling atol.
Declaring convergence at maxiter or after a small update even though the residual test failed.

selfTest.q: Which assumptions are used in the relative residual bound?
selfTest.a: Invertibility gives \(x^*-\hat{x}=A^{-1}r\). Consistent operator and vector norms give \(\|\text{error}\|\le\|A^{-1}\|\|r\|\) and \(\|b\|\le\|A\|\|x^*\|\). Combine them to get the relative bound; \(b\) and \(x^*\) must be nonzero to divide by their norms. No random or convergence assumption is needed.

selfTest.q: Why does multiplying A and b by the same nonzero scalar leave relative residual unchanged?
selfTest.a: Both \(\|r\|\) and \(\|b\|\) acquire the scalar's absolute magnitude. The solution is unchanged, but an absolute residual tolerance must be rescaled to preserve the same test exactly.

selfTest.q: Why do vanishing harmonic increments not establish convergence?
selfTest.a: \(H_{n+1}-H_n=1/(n+1)\) tends to zero. But each block from \(2^{k-1}+1\) through \(2^k\) contributes at least \(1/2\), because it has \(2^{k-1}\) terms each at least \(1/2^k\). Thus \(H_{2^k}\ge 1+k/2\), including \(k=0\), and the sums diverge.

selfTest.q: What does a primal-dual gap certify, and what must be checked first?
selfTest.a: For primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible multipliers, weak duality bounds \(f(x)-p^*\) by \(f(x)-g\). Check both feasibilities before interpreting the gap. Strong duality is needed to make arbitrarily tight such certificates possible, not for this lower-bound argument.

selfTest.q: What makes the contraction-mapping existence guarantee valid?
selfTest.a: A nonempty complete domain, such as a closed interval of \(\mathbb{R}\), an invariant map \(g(S)\) contained in \(S\), and a global Lipschitz constant \(q<1\). Invariance keeps all iterates in \(S\); the contraction bounds successive differences by a geometric sequence, hence the iterates are Cauchy. Completeness puts the limit in \(S\), and continuity gives \(g(p)=p\). The contraction also proves uniqueness. An open interval alone does not provide completeness.

practice.note: The harmonic sums in Reproduce are one answer; find a different foiling sequence and prove both properties. Explain why a shrinking update alone is insufficient, then specify finite-value, residual, stagnation and iteration-cap statuses for your own loop.
